entry.title: FP8 Block-wise Quantization for MoE
entry.summary: How 128×128 block-wise FP8 quantization works, what it fixes compared with a single per-tensor scale, and how vLLM and TensorRT-LLM load block-scaled MoE weights.
entry.content:
FP8 stores a number in one byte, half the size of BF16, and FP8 matrix multiplication runs at twice the BF16 rate on recent GPUs. The format has a much smaller range than BF16, so a tensor is scaled into that range before the cast and scaled back afterward. Block-wise quantization gives each 128×128 block of a weight matrix its own scale. DeepSeek-V3 trained and released its weights this way, and vLLM and TensorRT-LLM can serve such checkpoints directly.

The FP8 E4M3 format

The FP8 formats paper by Micikevicius et al. defines two encodings. E4M3 has 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits, and E5M2 has 5 and 2. The paper recommends E4M3 for weights and activations, which need precision, and E5M2 for gradients, which need range. PyTorch calls the E4M3 variant torch.float8_e4m3fn. The fn suffix means finite: the format has no infinity, and it uses the freed bit patterns to extend the largest value to 448.

With 3 mantissa bits, the gap between neighboring E4M3 values is 1/8 of a power of two. A cast rounds 100 to 96, for example. The normal values span from 2⁻⁶ (about 0.0156) to 448, a ratio of about 28,000. Smaller values become subnormal, with fewer significant bits, and values below 2⁻¹⁰ round to zero.

The cast

A scale maps the largest magnitude in a group of values to 448. The cast below comes from the tests of DeepGEMM, DeepSeek’s FP8 GEMM library (MIT license). It computes one scale per 128×128 block:

import torch
from typing import Tuple

def ceil_div(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    return (x + y - 1) // y

def per_block_cast_to_fp8(x: torch.Tensor) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    assert x.dim() == 2
    m, n = x.shape
    x_padded = torch.zeros((ceil_div(m, 128) * 128, ceil_div(n, 128) * 128),
                           dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device)
    x_padded[:m, :n] = x
    x_view = x_padded.view(-1, 128, x_padded.size(1) // 128, 128)
    x_amax = x_view.abs().float().amax(dim=(1, 3), keepdim=True).clamp(1e-4)
    x_scaled = (x_view * (448.0 / x_amax)).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn)
    return (x_scaled.view_as(x_padded)[:m, :n].contiguous(),
            (x_amax / 448.0).view(x_view.size(0), x_view.size(2)))

The function pads the matrix with zeros to a multiple of 128 in both dimensions. It then views the padded matrix as (m/128, 128, n/128, 128), so that dimensions 1 and 3 index the rows and columns inside a block. amax(dim=(1, 3)) finds the largest magnitude in each block. The clamp at 1e-4 keeps an all-zero block, such as one made entirely of padding, from dividing by zero.

The function returns two tensors. The first is the FP8 matrix with the original shape. The second holds one FP32 scale per block, with shape (ceil(m/128), ceil(n/128)). The original value is approximately the FP8 value times the scale of its block. A 4096×4096 weight has 1,024 blocks, so its scales take 4 KB next to 16 MB of FP8 data.

Per-tensor and per-block scales

A per-tensor scale maps the largest value in the whole matrix to 448. The rest of the matrix scales down with it, and small values can fall below the normal range of E4M3. A per-block scale confines that effect to the 128×128 block that holds the large value.

The experiment below measures how much this matters. It builds a 4096×4096 BF16 matrix with entries drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation 0.02, then places 64 outliers at a chosen multiple of that typical size. It quantizes the matrix both ways and measures the relative error of the non-outlier entries, together with the fraction of non-zero entries that the cast rounds to zero:

Outlier size Per-tensor error Per-block error Zeroed, per-tensor Zeroed, per-block
10× 2.65% 2.64% 0.0% 0.0%
100× 2.65% 2.64% 0.0% 0.0%
1,000× 2.65% 2.64% 0.2% 0.0%
10,000× 2.71% 2.65% 1.7% 0.1%
100,000× 12.59% 3.98% 17.2% 1.0%

Up to outliers about 1,000 times the typical value, both methods give the same error of about 2.6%. That error comes from rounding to 3 mantissa bits, and a finer scale cannot reduce it. Per-tensor scaling starts to lose small values only when the outliers approach the 28,000:1 normal range of E4M3. In that regime, per-block scaling keeps the error close to the rounding floor.

Trained weight matrices rarely have outliers that large. Activations can. LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al., 2022) found a few hidden dimensions with extreme magnitudes in every layer of transformers from about 6.7B parameters up. The DeepSeek-V3 technical report cites this sensitivity to activation outliers as the reason for fine-grained scaling. It quantizes activations in 1×128 tiles, one scale per token per 128 channels, computed at run time, and weights in 128×128 blocks.

Applying the scales in the matrix multiplication

In Y = X Wᵀ, the reduction runs over the hidden dimension in steps of 128. Within one step, every activation value shares one tile scale and every weight value shares one block scale. The kernel computes the FP8 partial product for the step and multiplies it by the two scales before adding it to an FP32 accumulator. The DeepSeek-V3 report describes this design and its second purpose. Tensor-core accumulation of FP8 products on H800 GPUs keeps fewer bits than FP32, so the kernel moves the partial sums to FP32 every 128 elements, which is also where the scales apply.

Block-scaled MoE checkpoints

An MoE layer has separate gate, up and down projection weights for each expert, and each of these matrices has its own block scales. The DeepSeek-V3 checkpoint declares the scheme in its config.json:

"quantization_config": {
  "quant_method": "fp8",
  "fmt": "e4m3",
  "activation_scheme": "dynamic",
  "weight_block_size": [128, 128]
}

dynamic means the activation scales are computed at run time. The weight documentation names the per-block scale tensor weight_scale_inv and stores it in FP32 next to each FP8 weight.

Serving frameworks read this configuration and select block-scaled kernels:

  • vLLM. The FP8 quantization method in fp8.py accepts weight_block_size. Setting the environment variable VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=1 routes supported FP8 GEMMs to DeepGEMM.
  • TensorRT-LLM. The quantization algorithm QuantAlgo.FP8_BLOCK_SCALES selects block scaling. Its PyTorch MoE layer, built by create_moe, has several backends. The TRTLLM backend supports only block-scaled FP8 or NVFP4 weights and falls back to the CUTLASS backend otherwise.

The kernels differ in speed by token count, so a comparison between backends sweeps the number of tokens from decode sizes up to prefill sizes.

References

  • FP8 Formats for Deep Learning (Micikevicius et al., 2022)
  • LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale (Dettmers et al., 2022)
  • DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report (DeepSeek-AI, 2024)
  • DeepGEMM tests/test_core.py
  • DeepSeek-V3 weight documentation
  • vLLM FP8 quantization method
  • TensorRT-LLM create_moe

entry.title: Segment Sums and Segmented Softmax
entry.summary: Segment sums reduce the rows of a tensor by group label. A segmented softmax built from them normalizes the scores of many packed sequences at once, and the way it is written decides whether a compiled graph grows with the number of sequences.
entry.content:
A segment sum adds up the rows of a tensor that share a label. Its inputs are a data tensor and a vector of segment IDs, one per row, and row s of the output is the sum of the data rows whose ID is s:

out[s] = sum of data[i] for every i where segment_ids[i] == s

The same pattern works with other reductions, such as max, min and mean. Frameworks expose it under different names. TensorFlow has tf.math.unsorted_segment_sum, JAX has jax.ops.segment_sum, and PyTorch has index_add_ and scatter_reduce_.

A small example

Six values in three segments:

import torch

data = torch.tensor([1., 2., 3., 4., 5., 6.])
ids = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2])
torch.zeros(3).index_add_(0, ids, data)
# tensor([ 3., 12.,  6.])

The segment IDs label rows, so a 2D input needs one ID per row, not one per element. Each row is reduced as a whole:

x = torch.tensor([[1., 2.], [3., 4.], [5., 6.]])
rid = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1])
torch.zeros(2, 2).index_add_(0, rid, x)
# tensor([[4., 6.],
#         [5., 6.]])

The number of segments sets the output shape. tf.math.segment_sum infers it from the largest ID and requires sorted IDs. The unsorted TensorFlow variant and the JAX function take num_segments as an argument. A compiled graph needs a fixed output shape, so code that will be compiled passes num_segments explicitly.

Segmented softmax

A softmax over each segment needs two segment reductions, a max for numerical stability and a sum for the denominator:

m[s]   = max of scores[i] in segment s
e[i]   = exp(scores[i] - m[segment_ids[i]])
out[i] = e[i] / (sum of e[j] in segment s)

Each segment’s outputs sum to 1, and the segments do not affect each other.

LLM serving with continuous batching produces this situation. The tokens or KV cache blocks of several sequences are packed along one dimension of a single tensor, and the attention softmax for each sequence must cover only that sequence’s entries. Here the segment ID of an entry is the sequence it belongs to.

transformers-neuronx, the AWS Neuron library for LLM inference, has a blockwise_softmax function for its paged KV cache. The function is in layers/attention_utils.py, published in December 2024. The logits have one row per active cache block, and block_to_seq maps each block to its sequence. The function first reduces within each block, then calls blockwise_reduce_max and blockwise_reduce_sum to combine the blocks of each sequence. Those two functions are segment reductions with block_to_seq as the segment IDs.

Three ways to write it

The three versions below compute the same result. They differ in how many operations they put into the graph and which hardware units do the work.

A loop over segments

The direct version masks out every other segment, reduces, and writes the result back to the rows of the current segment:

def softmax_loop(scores, ids, num_segments):
    out = torch.empty_like(scores)
    for s in range(num_segments):
        mask = ids == s
        m = torch.where(mask, scores, float("-inf")).max()
        e = torch.where(mask, torch.exp(scores - m), 0.0)
        out = torch.where(mask, e / e.sum(), out)
    return out

The two transformers-neuronx functions follow this structure. Each one loops over range(num_seqs), and each iteration emits a constant, a compare, a masked select, a reduction, a broadcast and a second masked select:

for seq_id in range(num_seqs):
    seq_full = hlo.full(seq_id, s32, o_sizes)
    seq_mask = hlo.equal(seq_iota, seq_full)
    masked_logits = hlo.masked_select(seq_mask, logits, zero)
    output_br = hlo.broadcast(hlo.reduce_sum(masked_logits, dim=0, keepdim=True), o_sizes, [0, 1, 2])
    output = hlo.masked_select(seq_mask, output_br, output)

This Python loop runs while the graph is being traced, so the compiled graph contains one copy of the body per sequence. With a maximum of 64 sequences, the two reductions together emit 768 HLO instructions where a fixed-size formulation needs a handful. The graph and its compile time grow with the batch size. Every copy also reads the full logits tensor, so the memory traffic grows with the number of sequences too.

Scatter and gather

A scatter with a reduction writes each entry into the slot of its segment and combines collisions with max or add. A gather with the segment IDs then reads each segment’s result back to its entries:

def softmax_scatter(scores, ids, num_segments):
    m = torch.full((num_segments,), float("-inf")).scatter_reduce(
        0, ids, scores, reduce="amax")
    e = torch.exp(scores - m[ids])
    denom = torch.zeros(num_segments).index_add_(0, ids, e)
    return e / denom[ids]

The graph has the same number of operations for any number of segments. XLA’s scatter instruction takes the combining function as an argument, so both the max and the sum map onto it. How fast scatter and gather run depends on the backend and on how well it handles data-dependent addresses.

One-hot matrix multiplication

A one-hot matrix onehot[i, s] is 1 when entry i belongs to segment s. Multiplying by its transpose sums each segment, and multiplying by the matrix itself broadcasts each segment’s value back to its entries:

def softmax_onehot(scores, ids, num_segments):
    onehot = torch.nn.functional.one_hot(ids, num_segments).to(scores.dtype)
    m = torch.where(onehot.bool(), scores[:, None], float("-inf")).amax(dim=0)
    e = torch.exp(scores - onehot @ m)
    return e / (onehot @ (onehot.T @ e))

The sums and broadcasts become matrix multiplications, which run on the matrix units of an accelerator. A max cannot be written as a matmul, so the max uses a masked reduction over an [entries, segments] tensor. That tensor is the cost of this version. Its size is the number of entries times the number of segments, times the size of any trailing dimensions. Many of the multiplications are by zero, which is acceptable when the matrix units would otherwise sit idle.

Checking the versions

The three functions agree, and each segment of the result sums to 1:

torch.manual_seed(0)
scores = torch.randn(10)
ids = torch.tensor([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3])
a = softmax_loop(scores, ids, 4)
b = softmax_scatter(scores, ids, 4)
c = softmax_onehot(scores, ids, 4)
assert torch.allclose(a, b) and torch.allclose(a, c)
assert torch.allclose(torch.zeros(4).index_add_(0, ids, a), torch.ones(4))

Choosing an approach

For a compiled graph, a loop whose trip count is a tensor size or a batch limit makes the graph grow with that size. The scatter and one-hot versions keep the operation count fixed. Scatter does the least arithmetic. The one-hot version runs on the matrix units and uses no data-dependent addressing, at the price of an [entries, segments] intermediate. Which one is faster depends on the backend, so the choice comes from measuring both at the batch sizes the server runs.

A fused attention kernel can avoid the segmented softmax altogether. If the kernel receives a mask that marks which cached positions each query may attend to, it can run an ordinary softmax with the masked positions set to a large negative value. The mask then keeps the sequences apart.

References

  • attention_utils.py in transformers-neuronx
  • tf.math.unsorted_segment_sum
  • jax.ops.segment_sum
  • torch.Tensor.scatter_reduce_

entry.title: Paged Attention and Chunked Prefill for LLM Inference
entry.summary: This post explains how Paged Attention and Chunked Prefill optimize memory and computation in vLLM by organizing key-value caches into dynamic blocks and processing input sequences in manageable chunks. It includes a simple walkthrough with tensor shapes and code to showcase their integration for LLM inference.
entry.content:
Large Language Models (LLMs) impose significant memory and compute demands during inference, particularly when handling long sequences or large batch sizes. To address these challenges, the vLLM system introduces two key optimization techniques - Paged Attention1 and Chunked Prefill2 that target memory efficiency at different stages of inference. This post examines these techniques, clarifying their roles, mechanisms, and interplay. We demonstrate that they can be jointly employed to optimize both the prefill and decoding phases without conflict. Through tensor shape analysis and execution flow, we illustrate how these strategies improve throughput and memory utilization.

Memory Bottlenecks in LLM Inference

Inference in autoregressive LLMs typically involves two phases:

  1. Prefill Phase: The model processes a prompt sequence, computes hidden states, and builds key-value caches for subsequent decoding.
  2. Decoding Phase: The model generates tokens autoregressively, using previously computed key-value caches.

Both phases can be memory-intensive. In the prefill phase, peak memory usage can spike when processing long sequences. In the decoding phase, the cumulative storage of key-value tensors can saturate memory, particularly in multi-user, high-throughput settings.

Paged Attention

Paged Attention is a memory management strategy that organizes key-value tensors into fixed-size blocks. Instead of pre-allocating memory proportional to the maximum possible sequence length, Paged Attention dynamically allocates and pages these blocks into memory as needed during attention score computation.

Mechanism

Let the input sequence have length L, batch size B, hidden size H, and number of heads nhead. Without Paged Attention, key-value tensors are stored as:

Keys, Values ∈ ℝB × L × nhead × dhead

Paged Attention partitions these tensors into blocks of size block_size. Each block stores:

Block Tensor ∈ ℝB × block_size × nhead × dhead

During attention computation at position t, only the relevant blocks containing key-value pairs from positions 0 to t − 1 are loaded into memory.

Example Illustration

Consider the following configuration:

  • Sequence length L = 12
  • Batch size B = 2
  • Hidden size H = 8
  • Number of heads n_head = 2
  • Head dimension d_head = 4 (since H = n_head × d_head)
  • Block size = 4

The key-value tensor shapes without Paged Attention would be:

Keys, Values ∈ ℝ2 × 12 × 2 × 4

With Paged Attention, the sequence is divided into:

  • Block 1: Positions 0–3 → Shape (2, 4, 2, 4)
  • Block 2: Positions 4–7 → Shape (2, 4, 2, 4)
  • Block 3: Positions 8–11 → Shape (2, 4, 2, 4)

When computing attention for position t = 9, the model dynamically loads:

  • Block 1: Positions 0–3
  • Block 2: Positions 4–7
  • First two positions of Block 3: Positions 8–9

Chunked Prefill

Chunked Prefill is an optimization technique applied during the prefill phase to control peak memory usage. It divides the input sequence into fixed-size chunks and processes them sequentially, limiting memory allocation for hidden state and key-value computation.

Mechanism

Given a sequence of length ( L ), the sequence is partitioned into chunks of size chunk_size. For each chunk:

  1. The model computes the hidden states for tokens within the chunk.
  2. It computes and caches the key-value tensors corresponding to these tokens.

Chunked Prefill performs full attention computation within each chunk, meaning each token’s query attends to all preceding tokens, including those in prior chunks.

However, during prefill, the model does not compute attention outputs for future decoding tokens; it only prepares the key-value cache required for the decoding phase.

Example

Using the same configuration:

  • Sequence length L = 12
  • Batch size B = 2
  • Hidden size H = 8
  • Number of heads n_head = 2
  • Head dimension d_head = 4
  • Chunk size = 6

The sequence is divided into:

  • Chunk 1: Positions 0–5
  • Chunk 2: Positions 6–11

For each chunk:

  • Hidden state tensor shape: (2, 6, 8)
  • Key-value tensor shape: (2, 6, 2, 4)

Attention Computation during Prefill:

For token at position t = 4 in Chunk 1, attention is computed over positions 0–3 within Chunk 1.
For token at position t = 7 in Chunk 2, attention is computed over:

  • Cached key-values from Chunk 1 (positions 0–5)
  • Tokens 6–6 (preceding tokens in Chunk 2)

Combined Example and Execution Flow

Let:

  • Sequence length L = 12
  • Batch size B = 2
  • Hidden size H = 8
  • Number of heads n_head = 2
  • Head dimension d_head = 4
  • Chunk size = 6
  • Block size = 4

Prefill Phase

The model processes:

  • Chunk 1 (positions 0–5):
    • Hidden states: (2, 6, 8)
    • Key-value tensors cached: (2, 6, 2, 4)
  • Chunk 2 (positions 6–11):
    • Hidden states: (2, 6, 8)
    • Key-value tensors cached: (2, 6, 2, 4)

Each token in Chunk 2 attends to all cached key-value pairs from Chunk 1 and preceding tokens in Chunk 2.

Decoding Phase

During decoding, suppose the model is generating token at position t = 12:

  • The model computes attention for the query at t = 12 over all cached key-value tensors from positions 0–11.
  • Key-value tensors are organized in blocks:

Paged Attention dynamically loads the necessary blocks during attention computation.

Block Positions Shape
1 0–3 (2, 4, 2, 4)
2 4–7 (2, 4, 2, 4)
3 8–11 (2, 4, 2, 4)


Tensor Shapes

Component Tensor Shape
Key/Value tensor (no paging) (B, L, n_head, d_head)
Key/Value tensor in Paged Attention (B, block_size, n_head, d_head) per block
Key/Value tensor in Chunked Prefill (B, chunk_size, n_head, d_head) per chunk

A simple structure of how block_size and chunk_size are utilized in attention mechanisms is provided below.

Paged Attention and block_size:

Paged Attention manages the Key-Value (KV) cache by dividing it into fixed-size blocks, allowing dynamic memory allocation and efficient handling of varying sequence lengths. The block_size parameter determines the number of tokens each block can store. In vLLM, this is evident in the attention backend implementations.

Example from flash_attn.py:

# Each block can contain up to block_size tokens.
block_tables: Optional[torch.Tensor]

In this snippet, block_tables is a tensor that maps sequences to their respective blocks in the KV cache, with each block capable of holding up to block_size tokens. This structure enables efficient memory usage by allocating only the necessary amount of memory based on the sequence length.

Chunked Prefill and chunk_size:

Chunked Prefill processes long input sequences by dividing them into smaller chunks, reducing peak memory usage during the prefill phase. The chunk_size parameter defines the size of these chunks. In vLLM, the attention backends handle chunking to ensure that memory constraints are respected during computation.

Example from pallas.py:

# Make sure the chunk size is a multiple of 2.
chunk_size = chunk_size // 2 * 2
num_chunks = (batch_size + chunk_size - 1) // chunk_size

Here, the code ensures that chunk_size is an even number and calculates num_chunks, the total number of chunks needed to process the batch. This approach allows the model to handle large sequences by processing manageable chunks sequentially, thereby optimizing memory usage.

Integration in Attention Computation:

The interplay between chunk size and block size exposes a tunable trade-off between latency and memory efficiency. A smaller chunk size reduces peak memory during prefill but may increase latency due to more sequential chunk processing. A smaller block size reduces persistent memory overhead but may increase the number of memory page operations, potentially affecting throughput.

Adaptive strategies that adjust chunk and block sizes based on sequence length, batch size, and memory pressure may further improve resource utilization. During attention computation, especially in scenarios involving long sequences or large batches, vLLM’s attention backends utilize both block_size and chunk_size to manage memory effectively. The KV cache is organized into blocks of size block_size, and input sequences are processed in chunks of size chunk_size. This dual approach ensures that the model can handle extensive inputs without exceeding memory limitations.

Example from flashinfer.py:

# Get the number of valid blocks based on sequence length.
block_table_bound = seq_len // self.block_size + 1 if seq_len % self.block_size != 0 else seq_len // self.block_size

This snippet calculates the number of valid blocks required for a given sequence length, ensuring that the KV cache is allocated appropriately. By managing the KV cache in blocks and processing input in chunks, vLLM effectively balances memory usage and computational efficiency during attention operations.

Sample code structure with Paged Attention and Chunked Prefill

To provide further clarity on the operational dynamics of Paged Attention and Chunked Prefill, the below includes a code walkthrough that models the mechanisms used in the vLLM system. The following Python code captures the essential logic behind how the key-value (KV) cache is organized into blocks and how input sequences are processed in chunks.

This example is based on the configuration discussed earlier:

  • Batch size B = 2
  • Sequence length L = 12
  • Hidden size H = 8
  • Number of attention heads n_head = 2
  • Head dimension d_head = 4
  • Block size 4
  • Chunk size 6
import torch

# Configuration
B = 2                     # Batch size
L = 12                    # Sequence length
H = 8                     # Hidden size
n_head = 2                # Number of heads
d_head = H // n_head      # Head dimension
block_size = 4            # Paged Attention block size
chunk_size = 6            # Chunked Prefill size

# Initialize key-value cache using block table
num_blocks = (L + block_size - 1) // block_size

# Each sequence in batch has its own block table mapping token idx to physical block
block_table = torch.arange(num_blocks).repeat(B, 1)  # [B, num_blocks]
kv_cache = torch.randn(B, num_blocks, block_size, n_head, d_head)  # KV store

# Dummy queries for current chunk
Q = torch.randn(B, chunk_size, n_head, d_head)

# Prefill processing loop (Chunked Prefill)
for b in range(B):
    for chunk_start in range(0, L, chunk_size):
        chunk_end = min(chunk_start + chunk_size, L)
        curr_chunk_len = chunk_end - chunk_start
        q = Q[b, :curr_chunk_len]  # [chunk_len, n_head, d_head]

        # Accumulate attention outputs
        attn_out = []

        # Compute attention over previous tokens using Paged Attention blocks
        for t in range(chunk_start, chunk_end):
            # For query at position t, get all keys from positions [0, t]
            t_block_idx = t // block_size

            context_keys = []
            context_values = []

            # Page in required blocks
            for blk_id in range(t_block_idx + 1):  # include current block
                physical_block = block_table[b, blk_id]
                kv_block = kv_cache[b, physical_block]   # [block_size, n_head, d_head]
                context_keys.append(kv_block)
                context_values.append(kv_block)  # simplified: keys = values

            # Flatten context into a single tensor [T', n_head, d_head]
            K = torch.cat(context_keys, dim=0)[:t+1]  # causal
            V = torch.cat(context_values, dim=0)[:t+1]

            q_t = q[t - chunk_start]  # query vector at position t

            # Scaled dot-product attention
            scores = torch.einsum("hd,thd->t", q_t, K) / (d_head ** 0.5)
            probs = torch.softmax(scores, dim=0)
            ctx = torch.einsum("t,thd->hd", probs, V)

            attn_out.append(ctx)

        # Stack outputs: [chunk_len, n_head, d_head]
        attn_out = torch.stack(attn_out, dim=0)
        print(f"Chunk [{chunk_start}:{chunk_end}] attention output shape:", attn_out.shape)

Operational Flow

  • The block_table holds logical-to-physical mappings of KV blocks for each sequence in the batch. Each block can store block_size tokens.

  • The KV cache (kv_cache) is allocated as [B, num_blocks, block_size, n_head, d_head].

  • For each chunk (driven by chunk_size), queries are processed in a causal way: each query t attends to all previous tokens (positions 0 to t), using the paged blocks.

  • Only the relevant blocks (from block 0 up to block ⌊t/block_size⌋) are paged in.

  • Attention is computed with the standard scaled dot-product mechanism using concatenated keys and values.

  • Paged Attention ensures that the key-value cache is organized into fixed-size blocks. Each token’s query accesses the minimum required set of blocks based on its position t. This reduces persistent memory footprint and supports dynamic allocation.

  • Chunked Prefill ensures that the input sequences are processed in chunks of size 6. For each chunk, attention scores are computed incrementally over all previously processed tokens, including those in earlier chunks. This limits peak memory usage during the prefill phase.

  • Dynamic Paging is setup such that for each token t in a chunk, only the blocks containing keys/values from positions 0 to t are loaded, ensuring efficient memory utilization.

Conclusion

Paged Attention and Chunked Prefill are orthogonal strategies for optimizing LLM inference in memory-constrained environments. Paged Attention reduces persistent memory consumption during attention score computation by dynamically paging key-value blocks. Chunked Prefill mitigates peak memory usage during the prefill phase by processing input sequences in chunks. There are also exploration around kernel-level optimizations, fused attention score computation across blocks, and dynamic eviction policies for the block table to further improve inference throughput under multi-user, long-sequence workloads.

References

  1. vLLM Paged Attention — vLLM. https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/kernel/paged_attention.html#vllm-paged-attention. Accessed 27 Mar. 2025.↩︎

  2. Optimization and Tuning — vLLM. https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/performance/optimization.html#chunked-prefill. Accessed 27 Mar. 2025.↩︎

entry.title: LLM Inference Systems
entry.summary: A quick clarification between the terms - Triton, TensorRT, and TensorRT-LLM
entry.content:
In my exploration of various inference systems, there is a general confusion about Triton, TensorRT, and TensorRT-LLM. These are all related to optimizing and deploying machine learning models, but with different purposes and use cases, specifically what inputs and outputs that they support.

Triton

Triton is an open-source inference server (NVIDIA) designed to optimize and deploy machine learning models for inference workloads and supports multiple deep learning frameworks, including TensorFlow, PyTorch, and TensorRT. Triton supportsfeatures like batching, concurrent model execution, and dynamic batching to improve performance and efficiency.

  • Inputs Triton can accept inputs in various formats, such as images, text, or numerical data, depending on the machine learning model being deployed.
  • Outputs The outputs depend on the specific machine learning model and its task, such as classification results, object detection bounding boxes, or text generation.

TensorRT

TensorRT is a high-performance deep learning inference optimizer and runtime library developed by NVIDIA designed to optimize and accelerate the inference performance of deep learning models on NVIDIA GPUs. TensorRT can optimize models from various deep learning frameworks, including TensorFlow, PyTorch, and ONNX.

  • Inputs TensorRT accepts deep learning models in various formats, such as TensorFlow frozen graphs, PyTorch traced models, or ONNX models.
  • Outputs TensorRT optimizes the models for faster inference on NVIDIA GPUs, but it does not change the model’s output format. The outputs remain the same as the original model, such as classification probabilities, object detection bounding boxes, or segmentation masks.

TensorRT-LLM

TensorRT-LLM is a branch of TensorRT specifically designed for optimizing and deploying large language models (LLMs) on NVIDIA GPUs. It provides optimizations and techniques tailored for the efficient inference of LLMs, which can be computationally expensive due to their large size and complex architectures.

  • Inputs TensorRT-LLM accepts pre-trained LLM models in various formats, such as TensorFlow, PyTorch, or ONNX.
  • Outputs The outputs of TensorRT-LLM remain the same as the original LLM model, which typically involves generating text based on the input prompt or context.

TL;DR - Triton is an inference server that can deploy and optimize models from different frameworks, including TensorRT-optimized models. TensorRT is a library for optimizing and accelerating deep learning models for inference on NVIDIA GPUs. TensorRT-LLM is a specialized branch of TensorRT focused on optimizing and deploying large language models efficiently on NVIDIA GPUs.

entry.title: Top-2 Logit Analysis for Accuracy Across Hardware
entry.summary: The gap between the top two tokens at each generation step shows where a model is uncertain, and where two hardware paths can select different tokens without either being incorrect.
entry.content:
When a model selects an unexpected token, the gap between the top two candidates at that step is a useful first measurement. A small gap indicates that the model is uncertain, and sampling at that step is close to a coin flip. A large gap indicates that the model is confident. Plotting the gap across all generation steps shows which steps are stable and which are sensitive to small numeric changes.

Step 1: dump logits offline

The TensorRT-LLM run.py script can write both context and generation logits to disk.

#!/bin/bash
# dump_logits.sh
# Generates a npy array on disk with the generated logits

script="run.py"
engine_dir="r8_trt_logits/8-gpu/"
input_csv="tokenizer_input.csv"

mpirun -np 8 --allow-run-as-root python ${script} \
  --input_file ${input_csv} \
  --output_csv outputs.csv \
  --output_logits_npy logits.npy \
  --top_p 1.0 \
  --temperature 1.0 \
  --max_output_len 100 \
  --engine_dir "${engine_dir}"

The flags have the following roles:

  • --input_file reads the tokenized input prompts from a CSV file.
  • --output_csv writes the generated text.
  • --output_logits_npy writes the per-step logits as a .npy file.
  • --top_p 1.0 --temperature 1.0 keeps the full distribution with no truncation.
  • --max_output_len 100 generates 100 output tokens.
  • mpirun -np 8 runs the engine across 8 GPUs with tensor parallelism.

The engine must be built with --gather_generation_logits, otherwise it does not return generation logits.

The resulting logits.npy has shape (batch_size, beam_size, token_gen_steps, vocab_size). For greedy decoding with beam_size=1 and batch_size=1, a 100-token generation produces a tensor of shape (1, 1, 100, vocab_size).

Step 2: analyze the deltas

The following script loads the dump and plots the gap:

# analyze_logits.py
import numpy as np
import torch
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import sys


def diff2(logits_at_step, step=-1):
    """Difference between the top-2 logits at a single step."""
    top2 = torch.topk(logits_at_step, 2).values
    print(f"step {step}: top2={top2}")
    return abs(top2[0].item() - top2[1].item())


def plot(values):
    df = pd.Series(values)
    df.plot(
        ylabel="diff of top two probabilities",
        xlabel="token generation steps",
        legend=False,
    )
    plt.hlines(y=0.0, xmin=0, xmax=len(values),
               colors='red', linestyles='-', lw=1,
               label='no diff in probs')


def main():
    gen_logits = torch.from_numpy(np.load(sys.argv[1]))
    batch_sz, beam_sz, token_gen_steps, vocab_size = gen_logits.shape
    print(f"logits shape: {gen_logits.shape}")

    logits_diff = []
    probs_diff = []
    for step in range(token_gen_steps):
        logits_at_step = gen_logits[0][0][step]
        logits_diff.append(diff2(logits_at_step, step))

        probs_at_step = torch.softmax(logits_at_step, dim=-1)
        probs_diff.append(diff2(probs_at_step, step))

        # When probabilities are exactly tied (which shouldn't happen in fp32):
        if probs_diff and probs_diff[-1] == 0:
            past_ids = torch.argmax(gen_logits[0][0], dim=1)[:step]
            print(f"  TIE at step {step}; previous tokens: {past_ids}")

    plot(probs_diff)
    plt.legend(loc="upper right")
    plt.show()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The script runs as python analyze_logits.py logits.npy.

It computes two values per step:

  • logits_diff is the gap between the top two raw logits. It measures the model’s confidence in raw units.
  • probs_diff is the gap between the top two probabilities after softmax. It measures how close the step is to a coin flip.

Reading the plot

Most plots contain three kinds of steps. The thresholds below are working heuristics, not fixed constants.

High-confidence steps have a probs_diff above 0.3. Greedy decoding and sampling produce the same token. On simple prompts, a well-trained model spends most of its steps in this range.

Borderline steps have a probs_diff between 0.05 and 0.3. The model prefers one token, but sampling can still select the second. Temperature affects the output at these steps.

Coin-flip steps have a probs_diff below 0.05. The top two tokens are nearly tied, so a different hardware path or a small numeric difference can change the sampled token. Divergence between CPU and Neuron, or between BF16 and FP32, tends to occur at these steps.

The shape of the whole curve also characterizes the model:

  • When nearly every step is high-confidence, the prompts lie well within what the model has learned, and its outputs repeat across runs.
  • When coin-flip steps are frequent, sampling produces varied outputs from run to run.
  • A bimodal curve indicates confident early steps, constrained by the prefix, followed by open-ended later steps.

Cross-hardware validation

When a Neuron model is validated against a GPU model, this analysis identifies where divergence is expected. The relevant quantity is the logit gap, because the numeric noise enters through the logits. Near a logit value of 20, one BF16 ULP is 0.125. When the top-two logit gap is within a few ULPs, the two hardware paths can rank the top two tokens differently, and neither result is incorrect. For two nearly tied tokens, a logit gap of 0.125 corresponds to a probability gap of at most about 0.06, so such steps already fall in the coin-flip range.

The validation procedure is as follows:

  1. Run the model on GPU as the reference and dump the logits.
  2. Run the model on Neuron as the target and dump the logits.
  3. For each step, read logits_diff from the reference run.
  4. If logits_diff is well above the expected logit error, for example several BF16 ULPs at the logit’s magnitude, the tokens are expected to match.
  5. If logits_diff is within that error, a token mismatch is acceptable.

Consider a run that diverges at step 47. If step 47 is a coin-flip step, the divergence is expected. If step 47 is a high-confidence step, the divergence indicates a real bug. The script distinguishes between the two cases. The compare_logits utility complements this check by measuring how the two logit tensors differ at a given step.

Probabilities or logits

The analysis can use either the raw logits or the probabilities after softmax.

The logits diff is easier to compare against the resolution of the data type. Near a logit value of 20, one BF16 ULP is 0.125, so a gap of 1.2 is well above the noise.

The probabilities diff maps directly to sampling behavior. If the top two tokens have probabilities 0.6 and 0.4, the diff is 0.2, and sampling at temperature 1.0 selects the second token 40% of the time.

Both values are inexpensive to compute, so the script records both.

Extending the analysis

With probs_diff available for every step, several further analyses require only a few lines of code.

A histogram of probs_diff across all steps summarizes the model’s confidence on a set of prompts. When most of the mass lies near zero, the output depends heavily on the sampling settings.

Per-step entropy, −Σ p log p over the full distribution, captures more information than the top-two gap.

Top-K agreement between two models compares the top-K token sets from two models at each step. It provides a finer measure of agreement than argmax alone.

Confidence after specific tokens tests whether the model becomes less confident after it produces certain tokens. This analysis can expose systematic sampling instability.

Practical notes

Memory. A 100-step generation with a 128k vocabulary in FP32 occupies about 50 MB per request. Storing the dump as float16 halves this, provided the analysis tolerates the lower precision.

MPI and multiple GPUs. In a tensor-parallel model, only rank 0 holds the gathered logits. The dump should be written from rank 0 only, otherwise each rank writes a partial copy.

Beam search. With beam_size > 1, the dump contains one distribution per beam. The analysis still applies, but each beam has its own confidence curve.

Sampling parameters. The dump contains the logits before top-p, top-k and temperature are applied. The analysis can therefore be repeated with different sampling settings without running the model again.
